name: Battle of Sagrajas
info: An Almoravid army under Yusuf ibn Tashfin, joined by the taifa kings of al-Andalus, defeated Alfonso VI of Castile near Badajoz in October 1086, easing Christian pressure on the taifas and opening the way for Almoravid rule in al-Andalus.

facts.date: 23 October 1086 (Friday, 12 Rajab 479 AH); Muslim sources say Alfonso VI had agreed to fight on the Monday
facts.place: The plain of Zallaqa or Sagrajas, north of Badajoz near the present border of Portugal, in the west of the Iberian Peninsula
facts.sides: The Almoravids under Yusuf ibn Tashfin and the taifa forces under Al-Mu'tamid ibn Abbad of Seville, with ten thousand Almoravid cavalry in the vanguard and 4,000 black troops among the Almoravids; Alfonso VI of Castile with allies from Aragon and elsewhere, his army put at 60,000
facts.outcome: The Muslim forces won and Alfonso VI fled by night to Coria. The sieges of major Andalusian cities were lifted, and Yusuf ibn Tashfin's standing in al-Andalus rose.

t: The Almoravids came to al-Andalus at the request of taifa rulers such as Al-Mu'tamid of Seville, after Alfonso VI took Toledo in 1085 and pressed on the other taifas.
Yusuf ibn Tashfin kept an elite reserve hidden behind a mound and attacked the Castilian camp while Alfonso's troops were pursuing the Andalusian line, and Alfonso broke off to save his camp.
Within about eighteen months of the battle the Almoravids had conquered the major cities of al-Andalus and ended the era of the taifa kings.
dyk: The Muslim army is said to have brought camels from Morocco whose sight and sound frightened the Castilian horses, and Arabic sources call the field az-Zallaqah, 'slippery ground', after the bloodshed there.
ev: Al-Mu'tamid ibn Abbad of Seville writes to Yusuf ibn Tashfin asking for help against Alfonso VI
Alfonso VI captures Toledo, which Muslims had held for 372 years, and takes lands along the Tagus
Yusuf ibn Tashfin takes Algeciras as his base and crosses into al-Andalus with his army
Alfonso VI proposes fighting on a Monday, and the armies camp either side of the Wadi Bira
The Muslim army defeats Alfonso VI at Sagrajas, and he escapes to Coria after dark
Yusuf ibn Tashfin returns to besiege Aledo and withdraws after four months
Yusuf ibn Tashfin crosses a third time and besieges Toledo, then lifts the siege for lack of supplies
Almoravid armies capture Córdoba, and Seville falls, ending the rule of the taifa kings

sections.background:
After the Fitna of al-Andalus the caliphate of Córdoba broke up into taifa kingdoms. The most powerful was Seville under the Banu Abbad; others included Toledo under the Dhulnunid dynasty, Zaragoza under the Banu Hud and Badajoz under the Banu al-Aftas. Their rulers were often more hostile to one another than to their Christian neighbours, and many bought military support from the northern kingdoms with tribute. Al-Mu'tamid ibn Abbad of Seville allied with Alfonso VI of Castile and paid him tribute in return for help against other taifa rulers.

In 1085 Alfonso VI captured Toledo, which Muslims had held for 372 years, and made it his capital. He also took the lands along both banks of the Tagus, including the fortresses of Madrid, Mérida and Badajoz, although Al-Mu'tamid warned him that this broke their agreement. Alfonso, with the intention of subjugating all the Muslim emirates, pressed on, and his forces besieged Zaragoza. Most Muslim rulers concluded that only the Almoravids of North Africa could help them.

The Almoravids were a Sunni Maliki reform movement of the Sanhaja tribes. Under Yusuf ibn Tashfin they controlled the western Maghreb from their capital Marrakesh. Al-Mutawakkil ibn al-Aftas of Badajoz and Al-Mu'tamid, who wrote in 1082, both appealed to him. Arabic sources add that Al-Mu'tamid had Alfonso's tax collector, Ibn Shalib, killed after an insult, and that a gathering at Córdoba then agreed to ask Yusuf for help. Yusuf's price was Algeciras, which Al-Mu'tamid gave up.
sections.forces:
The Muslim side was in two camps, the Andalusian and the Almoravid. Al-Mu'tamid was overall commander of the Andalusian forces, which included troops from Seville, from Almería under Ibn Sumadih, from Granada under Abdallah ibn Buluggin with his brother Tamim of Málaga, and from Badajoz under Al-Mutawakkil ibn al-Aftas. Al-Mu'tamid led the vanguard with Dawud ibn Aisha and ten thousand Almoravid cavalry. Al-Mutawakkil held the right flank, troops of eastern al-Andalus the left, and the rear was the other Andalusian forces. Yusuf ibn Tashfin kept the reserve, an elite group of Almoravid fighters from Morocco and his personal guard.

The 4,000 black soldiers in the battle are called hasham, paid mercenaries, by Ibn Khallikan, which suggests they were not slaves. According to Ibn 'Idhari, Yusuf had bought black slaves in 1071-1072 and added about 2,000 of them to his cavalry. Umar al-Naqar suggests they may have come from the Muslim kingdom of Takrur. Yusuf also had camels brought from Morocco, intended to unsettle the Frankish cavalry.

Alfonso VI had volunteers from southern France and Italy as well as men from Aragon, Galicia, Asturias and Biscay. His army is put at 60,000. He divided it in two. Count García and Count Zodric led the first division, to attack the Muslim vanguard. The second had two wings under Sancho Ramírez of Aragon and Count Raymond, with Alfonso at the centre and Albaráns commanding the vanguard. The armies faced each other across the Wadi Bira.
sections.course:
Alfonso arrived in Rajab 479 AH (October 1086) and, on a Thursday, proposed battle for the Monday. According to Yusuf's letter to Al-Mu'izz ibn Badis, he gave as his reason that Friday was the Muslim holy day, Saturday the Jewish and Sunday the Christian one. The Muslims suspected treachery and set scouts to watch. On the morning of Friday 23 October (12 Rajab) they reported that Alfonso was mobilising, and Al-Mu'tamid called on Yusuf for help.

Alfonso sent García and Zodric to strike Al-Mu'tamid's camp. They met the Almoravid cavalry of Dawud ibn Aisha first, who with many archers drove back the first attack but took losses. The front line of Al-Mu'tamid's Andalusians then gave way, and some Andalusian leaders fled to Badajoz, while Al-Mu'tamid and the knights of Seville held on, surrounded. Alfonso next attacked Ibn Aisha's men, reached the Almoravid tents and crossed the trench in front of them. Yusuf had sent a battalion under Sir ibn Abi Bakr, which broke into the Castilian army and joined Al-Mu'tamid.

While the Castilians chased Al-Mu'tamid, Yusuf rode with his reserve against the Castilian camp, where horses panicked at the camels, and he set the camels on fire. Alfonso broke off the pursuit to save his camp. Al-Mu'tamid's men and those who had fled to Badajoz then attacked, and 4,000 black cavalry from Takrur charged with lamta shields and javelins. One of them wounded Alfonso severely in the thigh, which left him with a limp. At sunset Alfonso withdrew to a hill and fled in the dark to Coria.
sections.aftermath:
Alfonso, who had arrived with an army of 60,000, retreated to a mountain fortress with around 300 knights. Spanish historians stress that his defeat was catastrophic and that he escaped in a pitiful state with a few companions. The sieges of the major Andalusian cities were lifted. Yusuf ordered a proclamation of the victory to be read in mosques across North Africa, and Al-Mu'tamid told his son in Seville.

Yusuf stayed near Seville for three days and then returned to Morocco because his son and heir Abu Bakr had died, and he feared instability in the Maghreb. Before leaving, he urged the Andalusian rulers to unite, according to Ibn Buluggin, and left 3,000 Almoravid soldiers with Al-Mu'tamid. Sir ibn Abi Bakr, appointed to lead the Almoravid forces in al-Andalus, went with Al-Mutawakkil into central Portugal as far as the Tagus. Al-Mu'tamid took several fortresses near Toledo but was pushed back in Murcia by El Cid's knights.

The rulers fell back into disputes, and the Castilians resumed raiding from the fortress of Aledo. Yusuf returned in 1088 to besiege it, withdrew after four months, and returned again in 1090. Over the following years the Almoravids deposed the taifa kings. Abdallah ibn Buluggin of Granada and then Al-Mu'tamid were captured and sent to Aghmat.
sections.sources:
The battle is known mainly from Arabic sources and later Muslim historians. They preserve letters between the Andalusian rulers, Yusuf ibn Tashfin and Alfonso VI, and the words of Ibn Buluggin, Ibn al-Kardabus and the poet al-Hamiri. Yusuf's letter to Al-Mu'izz ibn Badis is the source for the agreement to fight on Monday and for Alfonso's supposed plan to attack early. Joseph Aschbach, a German historian, wrote that Alfonso thought he might use deceit in war and break a sworn pact.

The names differ with the tradition. Muslim sources call it the Battle of az-Zallaqah, from the plain, and the Arabic name is said to mean slippery ground. In European accounts the first phase, against Al-Mu'tamid and Dawud ibn Aisha, is the Battle of Rueda and the second, against Yusuf, the Battle of Sacralias. Historians also disagree about the black troops, whether paid mercenaries or slaves and from where.
sections.legacy:
Muslim writers treated the battle as a great deliverance. Muhammad ibn al-Samak al-Amili wrote that it was a day unmatched since Yarmouk and Qadisiyyah. Ibn al-Kardabus said the stranglehold on the peninsula was eased, and Ibn Buluggin that since that day the Christians had been filled with fear. Before the battle, Andalusian rulers had been paying tribute to their Christian neighbours, and afterwards Yusuf was hailed as a saviour and his name was invoked in mosques. His influence grew across both al-Andalus and the Maghreb.

Spanish historians stress the scale of Alfonso's defeat, though he went on launching new offensives and never again had the same success. The battle halted Christian expansion for a time and preserved al-Andalus from Alfonso's Reconquista efforts.

The political result ran against the taifa kings who had called for help. The rulers returned to their quarrels, Yusuf crossed again in 1088 and 1090, and within eighteen months the Almoravids had conquered Granada, Málaga, Jaén, Córdoba, Seville, Almería, Valencia, Badajoz and the Balearic Islands. That ended the era of the taifa kings and began Almoravid control of al-Andalus.

summary: At Sagrajas, or az-Zallaqah, on 23 October 1086 Almoravid and Andalusian forces under Yusuf ibn Tashfin and Al-Mu'tamid defeated Alfonso VI of Castile, who fled by night to Coria. The victory halted his advance but was followed by Almoravid conquest of the taifa kingdoms.
notes: The article gives no casualty figures for either side and states Alfonso's 60,000 without attribution; the text gives only 60,000 arriving and around 300 knights retreating.
The article's 'Consequences' section says Alfonso retreated to a 'mountain fortress' and its Battle section says he fled to Coria; both are given.

Left out as garbled: the sentence about Count Gómez with 40,000 infantry and 20,000 cavalry 'ultimately resulting in the forced opening of Seville' (ends with a stray lower-case 'ultimately'); I used only the 'forced opening of Seville in 484 AH (1091 CE)' idea in a general form.
The 'Status of the Almoravids' section dates Marrakesh's foundation to 1062 and the entry into Fez to 1063; left out as inconsistent in order.
The article treats Alfonso's treachery on the day as fact in places and as Muslim report in others (Yusuf's letter, Aschbach); I attribute it.
'Decisive' and 'monumental' in the article are not used in the text.
The ev entry '1086' for the crossing is inferred from the sequence: the article dates Ibn Abbad's last letter to 479 AH and the battle to October 1086, but gives no year for the crossing itself.
The article describes the Almoravids' camels being set ablaze by Yusuf in the camp; the dyk says only that camels frightened the horses.
